utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone, both in and just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue your examination-in-chief of Witness Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Neskovic. May I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we move on to the next document, I wanted to ask you one additional question about the document found at tab 12 and in connection with the Variant A and B document found at tab 11. So can I ask you first to turn to tab 11 and look quickly at item 9 of the first level Variant A. And that provides, "Prepare an estimate of the number of necessary active and reserve policemen, TO units, and civilian protection units, and on that basis bring them up to full manpower levels and take any other necessary action for their engagement in keeping with the developments." May I ask you next to turn to tab 12 and look at item 9, reflected in the minutes of the 23 December 1991 meeting of the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo. That provides that "Persons responsible for item 9 are Drago Kovac, Milanko Jovanovic, and Momir Garic." And can you tell the Court who those persons were and what positions they occupied. To the right of their name on this particular document, we see civilian protection, MUP, and TO. And can you tell us whether that -- whether or not those are accurate reflections of the positions they occupied at the time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milanko Jovanovic was the chief of the police station in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. Drago Kovac was some sort of official in the Territorial Defence Staff in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo because according to the former law, the municipality had authority over territorial units and the Territorial Defence. And Momir Garic, I don't know whether at the time he worked in the Territorial Defence together with Kovac; it's possible. But I think that Drago Kovac and Momir Garic were from the Territorial Defence in Novo Sarajevo; whereas, Jovanovic was the chief of the Novo Sarajevo police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to turn next to tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 13 is already in evidence, P529, Hanson tab 260.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are the minutes of the Crisis Staff meeting of 29 January 1992, which was held at the Lukavica local community. As we see in the first paragraph, the attendees are listed. The meeting was opened by Mr. Bogdanovic, the deputy commander of the Crisis Staff. And then there are 11 items enumerated, including assembly point, tasks, storage depot, evacuation plans, et cetera. May I ask you to look in particular at item 11, which lists a task, and that task is to provide larger quantities of food and medicments and to transfer them to a safe location, make contacts with the company managers. In charge are Radomir Bogdanovic, Milivoje Prijic, Mr. Nastic, and Mr. Sojic. And can I ask you whether or not those -- that is, the -- essentially the same task and the same persons assigned that is reflected in item 7 of the December 23rd, 1991, meeting.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These tasks do overlap to a certain extent. There is something lacking in this document, and that is the case in the previous document, too. We can't see who the chief of the Crisis Staff was. We can't see who was at the head of the staff. I remember this meeting. I attended it; although, I did not participate in it very actively because these are matters that I was not very familiar with. But as far as I can remember, or given what I can see, I think that this is some sort of a plan for the evacuation of the Serbian population from certain local communes in the event of a crisis or of a war or something like that because item 11 is, in a certain respect, related to item 6. Under item 6, we can see that there are evacuation plans, and then the various local communes from which people would be evacuated are listed. Under item 11, it says, "Provide quantities of food and medical supplies. Transfer them to safe locations." So it is obvious that there was an evacuation plan here, a plan to evacuate some of the Serbian population from parts of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. And as in the case of the previous document, there is something that seems to be missing in this document, too. I don't quite understand why such a serious large-scale plan is being discussed at the Crisis Staff meeting of a local commune. Perhaps such a serious issue would be discussed at the municipal level, in a Municipal Staff. But I can't see who the commander or the chief of the Crisis Staff was; that seems to be missing. But I believe that this concerns an evacuation plan. Reference is also made to a warehouse; the courier system is also mentioned, and I think the communications between various bodies is also mentioned. This is a plan for the evacuation of the Serbian population from certain local communes in the event of war or in the event of some other kind of crisis. That's my understanding of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the attendees, Mr. Neskovic, including Mr. Djurovic, Mr. Prijic, and most, if not all, of those persons who were assigned tasks at the first meeting, and bear in mind the position of Mr. Bogdanovic, is this a subsequent meeting of the Crisis Staff, a follow-up meeting of the Municipal Crisis Staff held after the December 23rd, 1991, meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's related to that. Could I just add something? Something seems to be missing here again. Could we just discuss this document a little longer. I can't see who the chief of the Crisis Staff was; that seems to be missing. And operative duties are distributed in the Municipal Crisis Staff, so then there should be a session of the Crisis Staff where a report should be submitted on the tasks carried out. I can't see this other document. If individuals carried out their operative duties, then at some other meeting it would be necessary for them to submit a report stating what they had done. I also believe that this second document is missing. But reference is made to the second meeting of the Crisis Staff, but I can't see who the president of the Crisis Staff is, who the commander is. Here it says that Bogdanovic is one of the members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe it also indicates that the meeting -- the minutes of the meeting of 29 January that Bogdanovic was not only a member but the deputy commander. Do you have any independent recollection of who the commander of the Crisis Staff was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that I can't remember who the commander was. I should remember who he was. I would have known such a person. According to plan A and B, it should have been Zarko Djurovic, but these documents seem to show that Zarko Djurovic perhaps did not attend the meeting on the 19th of December, and perhaps he did not personally receive plans A and B, so perhaps that plan was delivered to the municipality of Novo Sarajevo by courier. But Djurovic's conduct was a little specific in this case. He tried to remain loyal and to abide by the orders of the leadership. But on the other hand, he tried to obstruct matters, not to carry out all the tasks because he didn't agree with everything. So the role he played was quite specific, and by virtue of his position, he should be here, but he wasn't presiding over the meeting of this Crisis Staff. Bogdanovic played an important role here, so don't hold this against me, but there is something missing here. We can't see who established the Crisis Staff, we can't see who its commander was, and we can't see who assigned these tasks to various groups. And I was in one group and was assigned tasks too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Neskovic - and I'm going to move away from that document at this point - you testified that there was a major problem in Novo Sarajevo between the party and the government of Mr. Djurovic, who was the president of the Executive Board, and testified about a conflict between Djurovic, as the head of the Municipal -- or the Executive Committee, and the president of the SDS party, who I think you recalled was Mr. Prijic. Now, if I recall correctly, you stated it was a problem of such a scope that Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic had to intervene and that they attended a meeting of the Municipal Board in person to use their personal authority to solve the problem. Let me now ask you a question or two about the conflict between Djurovic and Prijic. You also told us yesterday about Mr. Djurovic's contacts with the leadership and that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik knew him. Did Mr. Djurovic ask Dr. Karadzic and/or Mr. Krajisnik to use their authority on his behalf in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict was really on a large scale, and those who followed Milivoje Prijic were better organized, and they behaved in a slightly more extreme way. So I think that they managed to replace Djurovic in the conflict, and when Karadzic and Krajisnik arrived, I think that the two of them managed to calm the situation down, and that meant maintaining the status quo -- that meant that Djurovic would remain the president of the municipal authority. Without their help, I don't think Djurovic would have managed to hold onto his position as president of the municipal authorities. So Karadzic and Krajisnik did not openly enter into a conflict with either of the parties, but they used their authority to calm the situation down, to maintain the status quo, and the status quo was welcomed by Djurovic because they maintained his position. They calmed the situation down. They helped Djurovic, and he held onto that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand from your testimony that Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik intervened in the manner you just described. My question was a little bit different, and that is whether or not Mr. Djurovic reached out to or himself sought the assistance of Mr. Krajisnik or Dr. Karadzic in order to get them to intervene in this manner.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before that meeting was held he contacted Krajisnik, his office, and the Assembly - and I don't know whether Karadzic attended that meeting, too - as far as I know, he contacted him to obtain assistance from him before that meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look next at tab 18, please. Oh, before -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can this be marked next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P913.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, P913 is the minutes from the 13th Extraordinary Session of the Municipal Board of the SDS party Novo Sarajevo held on 28 February 1992. And if I may, I'd like to direct your attention to a couple of portions of that, but let me give you just a moment to look at that document quickly. As I think you can see from even a quick review of the document, there's a great deal of discussion about Dr. Prijic in particular. Let me first direct your attention to the second paragraph under agenda item 1, which is found at page 3 of the English translation and, I believe, can also be found at page 3 of the Serbian copy. That states at the -- toward the bottom of the page, "This also happened at the last meeting of Municipal Board, which was attended by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik." Is that a reference to the meeting you were talking about earlier, or is that another meeting attended by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik? I'll give you a moment to find the reference. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find that part. I'm not sure where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, when the witness is finding the exact location, on your list P913 appears as the minutes of the 13th Irregular Session; whereas, the document itself calls it an extraordinary. I don't think it's exactly the same. May I take it that "extraordinary" would be the right description?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, if you would take that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, if it's helpful, I think that's at -- that's at the page 3 of the Serbian version, and there is some identification numbers at the top of that page, which are SA029201.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then if you look down, you'll see agenda item 1 or AD1. And I'm referring to the second full paragraph, where there's a reference at what appears to be in the English the last sentence of that paragraph, that says, "This also happened at the last meeting of Municipal Board, which was attended by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question was whether that was a reference to the meeting that you had mentioned in your earlier testimony or another meeting attended by Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this concerns the meeting that I have mentioned. As far as I know, they only attended one meeting, and I think that this concerns the meeting that I was referring to a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention next to page 6 of the English version, and I think it's page 7 of the Serbian version. Just above agenda item 2, there is a reflection of the results of this meeting, indicating that Dr. Prijic was relieved of his post as president of the Municipal Board, that Mr. Gajevic was tasked with running the board until the next session, and that Karadzic and Krajisnik will be informed about this decision. And, again, is that a reference to the same conflict, same dispute you were talking about earlier and the resolution of that dispute with the termination of Dr. Prijic and the retention of Mr. Djurovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to know the nature of the conflict between Mr. Prijic and Mr. Djurovic. On page 4 of the document shown to you by the Prosecution, line 3 on page 4, I can see that it seems that Mr. Kutalj [phoen] is being referred to - I apologise for the pronunciation - and it says, "[In English] ... make any efforts to achieve separation of Serbian local communities from the administration division of local communities are people who belong to Dr. Prijic's clan." [Interpretation] So what is Dr. Prijic being criticised for? Could you provide us with any clarification in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, three factors were concerned. Firstly, Dr. Prijic believed that as a party they should have influence over party members in the executive bodies. That meant that they should consult the party, especially when personnel matters were concerned. Djurovic was of a different opinion. He thought that the president of the Executive Board of the municipality, that he was that president, that the government was a multi-ethnic one. The municipality had about 100.000 inhabitants; it was a very large municipality. To be the head of the government is a very important position, and he wanted to act in accordance with the municipality statute, without the party, and he didn't want to obey the Municipal Board of the SDS. That was one of the reasons. And the second reason is that there were a lot of flats and jobs in office premises in the municipality, so it was very important for someone to have influence on the Executive Board. And the third reason is that they were both Montenegrins; they weren't Bosnians. So they had old scores to settle that I'm not familiar with. And there's another reason: Dr. Prijic was a respected manager of Galenika, a pharmaceutical company, dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina, dealing with the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Kosovo, and he had a tendency to control everything. And then when this conflict with Djurovic became, Prijic started gathering people who were dissatisfied with the power structure, and the other person started gathering people around him who were content with the power structure and who were already members of that structure. So finally Prijic was replaced, and Djurovic came out of the conflict victorious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are referring to the part of the minutes that I had indicated to you. It's page 4. In the English version of the text, it's the second line. And we're talking about Mr. Kutalj, who's speaking here. And he says -- can you see that bit of the text? So he says, [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "Dr. Prijic is not to be relieved of his post. Chaos is going to prevail."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: ... make any efforts to achieve separation of Serbian local communities from the administration division of local communities are people who belong to Dr. Prijic's clan." [Interpretation] Now, I'd like you to comment on that sentence; that is to say, with regard to efforts to accomplish a separation between the Serb community and the administration of the local community. What does it actually mean, and what was the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this had been an ongoing feud, and it went all the way down to the local community, so there were local communities with Prijic supporters prevailed. That was the case in the local community such as Lukavica, Tilava, and other suburban areas. And then there were other local communities which tended to support Djurovic. So that Gotalj [phoen], I think he was from Grbavica, which is an urban community. So they kind of institutionalised the entire conflict because they said, Okay; unless this happen, then we'll take out local communities out of the area of competence of the municipal government, and we'll no longer obey them, as it were. And so it had actually become fully institutionalized, and basically the local communities are being misused and taken advantage of, in terms of settling this conflict. And so there was a division between the local communities, as well, in two camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, can I follow up on Judge Hanoteau's question and direct your attention to another portion of that same page, a little further down. I'll check to see if that's in the same page of your version, if I can. In any event, the portion I'm referring to states: "Dr. Prijic was not present during plebiscite. He did not protest when Muslims and Croats placed posters for their referendum in offices. Immigrants from Sandzak started illegal building of houses, and Dr. Prijic did not take any action to stop them." Now, this complaint against Dr. Prijic about his failure to take any action to stop the immigrants from Sandzak from constructing houses, is that the same issue that was referred to in the telephone conversation between Mr. Djurovic and Dr. Karadzic that was discussed yesterday, that November 1991 telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You also made reference to a multi-ethnic government at that time. So is it correct to say that a Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo had not yet been declared by that time? And in that connection, can I ask you to turn quickly to tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document at tab 22, Your Honours, is P826, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Neskovic, P826, tab 3, found at -- found in this binder at tab 22 is an April 1st, 1992, addition of Vicani Novani [phoen] from Sarajevo regarding the decision from foundation of Serbian Municipality Novo Sarajevo. The first sentence of that article states that "The founding session of Serbian people of municipality of Novo Sarajevo held on last Thursday." So since this is a Wednesday addition, without making the mathematical calculation, I take that to be sometime in the latter part of March 1992. Does that correctly reflect the date of the establishment of the Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at that founding Assembly; I think it was by the end of March. It happened at the memorial centre at Vrace. It is a place where quite a few Jews lost their lives in the Second World War. And there were the representatives of the city authorities from the SDS, and it was about setting up the Serb Municipality of Novo Sarajevo, who was meant to be merged with the Romanija area or something like that. And so the Assembly was held, but it was a bit of a failure, in fact. The Serb Municipality was not actually set up. Mr. Djurovic was basically perhaps trying to show that he was doing something. He wanted to be seen to be doing something, but he wasn't all that in favour. The others started arguing about who the president was going to be, and still others talked about territorial issues, as to where the government should be from. And after about an hour, an hour and a half of discussions, it all ended in a fray, basically. So there had been an attempt to set up the Serb Municipality, but it never came about because this meeting ended in failure, and obviously it transpired, however, and was reported in the media, but probably the journalists did not know about the details. And so there was a huge void which ensued, and this Serb Municipality of Novo Sarajevo actually was set up only as late as the 10th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, have you finished with this? Because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. otherwise I'd like to take the witness back to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, could I take you back to the previous document we find under tab 18, and could I invite you -- could I draw your attention to page 3, in the first paragraph under AD1. Do you see there the words "Bane Surbat," which is a name? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read slowly from that portion down the whole of the paragraph, so on from the line where it reads "Bane Surbat." Yes, please, could you read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "As of three days ago, in the municipal" -- "in the local community" - sorry - "Bane Surbat, there was a meeting which was interrupted because of the fact that Dr. Prijic allowed himself to engage in a physical settling of accounts with one of those present. So apart from doing the work of the Municipal Board, we also got a glimpse of bad human relations which culminated at that meeting, was stressed by Andric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you noted, Mr. Tieger, there's a whole line missing of the translation. This, of course, raises some concern about the quality of the translation of these documents. There's a whole line just not there. "After the fight with one of the representatives," then it continues in the translation with who took part in the discussion, which is, in the original, the next three lines, but there's just two lines missing. The reference to Andric is missing, who did what. The whole part -- "So apart from doing the work of the Municipal Board, we also got a glimpse of about" -- I mean, that's just not there. Of course, you didn't make the translation, so when I'm looking at you, it's not because I blame you personally for it, but it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I understand, Your Honour. And I'm not -- well, I mean obviously -- obviously we'll address this specific problem, and in the course of doing so we'll -- we'll try to step back and do as much of a systemic overview as we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to try to prevent problems like this in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I wanted to turn next to a document produced sometime, approximately two months or so, after the decision to establish the Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo that you spoke of a moment before. And in that connection, can I ask you to turn to tab 23, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 23 is P529, Hanson tab 158. It is a report on activities by the Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff directed to the attention of the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and bears the signature line for Mr. Neskovic, as president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, was this a report on the activities of the Crisis Staff that you prepared and submitted to the president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document in question. That's the document that I drafted as a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the problems that you described earlier in connection with the establishment of the Novo Sarajevo -- or the Serbian Municipality of Novo Sarajevo, you assumed the duties of president of this Crisis Staff and were reporting to the president of the Presidency about the activities undertaken by the Crisis Staff during that time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, just to make an indispensable clarification. Prior to this Crisis Staff, another Crisis Staff had been set up, headed by Mr. Djurovic, and I was a member of that Crisis Staff. And there were about 15 of us, and we were in a building in the vicinity of this memorial centre, and we were all assigned our tasks. And that was the first and the last meeting, in fact. Following that meeting, when we went out to do our work, I was in charge of the reparations to buildings, business facilities, and all that. Well, everybody scattered, basically, and left. Djurovic went to Belgrade, another one went somewhere else in Serbia, and the other members of the Crisis Staff simply fled. And I myself and Mirko Sarovic were the only ones left behind, and so that original Crisis Staff basically disappeared completely. And I believe at that time Djurovic was referring to a government decision or a set of instructions regulating the work of the Crisis Staffs on that occasion. But then Sarovic and myself found ourselves in a pickle because all the other officials had fled, and the top levels of the Serb Democratic Party from Sarajevo had fled, as well. And so whoever could, left. And Sarovic and I were trying to decide what to do, and we met there, and there were about 50 or 60 citizens who were in that area. And we decided we should set up a new Crisis Staff, and I was elected the president, and Sarovic remained a secretary because he was a legal expert. And on that occasion we decided to set up a Crisis Staff and to do our work as we best could, depending on the actual circumstances, and not to ask for any instructions from any higher authorities or anything. And so we did it of our own accord, and we tried to adapt our work to the situation at any given time, and we never asked for guidance or instructions from anyone else. And after two months or so, I think Mr. Karadzic had invited all the representatives of those Crisis Staffs Jahorina to the Bistrik Hotel in order for them to report on their work. And mostly it was oral presentations, and I actually drafted a written report. And so this date basically stood to indicate the date on which this Crisis Staff ceased to exist because on the 10th of June the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Committee was set up. So basically at the end of the period in the course of which we worked for the Crisis Staff, I drafted this report, and I think I submitted it to Karadzic personally, and I think Ostojic was sitting next to him, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to return to that document in just a minute, but I want to ask you about another meeting first. And I'd like to direct your attention to the period of time when -- or around the period of time when the airport was handed over to the French Batallion and ask whether you and others submitted a letter to the leadership at that time.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- what was the letter about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a huge meeting, organised at the Presidencies of the Energoinvest company at Lukavica, and it was chaired by the government commissioner for new Sarajevo, Mr. Milimir Mucibabic. Different groups of people attended that meeting: the representatives of the armed forces, the representatives of the police force, private citizens, soldiers, members of the Municipal Crisis Staff and government, et cetera. So it was a varied meeting with a picturesque attendance, and it was rather difficult. A great deal of criticism was voiced in the direction of the leadership at Pale, and the Presidency in the sense -- when we said "Presidency," what we meant was Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic and Koljevic, and a great deal of dissatisfaction was expressed with regard to the government, as well. Now, this was not what you could call a compact meeting. Whoever had a grudge would air their grievances, and so then it was all listed. And as far as I can remember, there were seven or eight requests that were addressed to the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at Pale; that is to say, Krajisnik, Biljana, Nikola, and Karadzic. And I think there was something from the army. They were unhappy about the fact that the airport was relinquished to UNPROFOR and placed under their control, and they expressed their dissatisfaction at that. Another group of reserve or non-commissioned officers were unhappy that their salaries were lower than those of the officers in active service. Other people were unhappy because there was a lot of looting, a lot of theft going on, stealing and everything, so they felt that a state of emergency or war should be introduced in order to introduce some order. And then Mr. Prijic -- or rather, other people were also unhappy about the fate of Sarajevo because within the city there had been rumours about Sarajevo being left to the Bosniaks completely and that the Serbs were going to leave it altogether, and there were 180.000 Serbs there. Even though, I mean, it was just a rumour, it still sent shock waves through the population. And I think that Mr. Prijic raised one issue. I think it was item 3 at the meeting, in fact. And he was arguing against the political legitimacy of the leadership of the Serb Bosnia and Herzegovina. He felt that they were traitors and that they betrayed the Serb national interests, and he suggested that we from the municipality should get in touch with other municipalities directly and agree with them about setting up some different -- some new Serb policy. So no matter whether you agreed or disagreed with any of those items, it was all referred to in a document. Everybody made their own contributions, and then we signed it in order to testify to the accuracy of all that. And I think there were 18 of us who signed the document, and then we sent it off. And after that document, there was a meeting that we had with the leadership, with the Serb Bosnia-Herzegovina at Pale, and on that occasion we talked about those requests. Unfortunately, I have not managed to hang onto that document. I did keep it for a long time, but then when I moved house, I somehow mislaid it. But there were about seven to eight different requests coming from different groups, and what is of interest in this respect is that the government commissioner, Mr. Mucibabic, seemed to support us in all that. He lent his support to everything we had to say. He, too, seemed to believe that that policy should be criticised. And so that encouraged the others, since there was somebody there on behalf of the government and he was encouraging us, and that encouraged people to come forward and make their points. After that, I think Mucibabic got a bit scared of the possible consequences of such actions, and I think he actually fled to Belgrade or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people actually -- from the municipality actually went to the meeting? You said about 18 signed it. How many showed up at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There were at least 50 to 60 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, you explained that. I didn't mean at the original meeting, but when there was the meeting with the leadership, how many people who had been at the original meeting went to meet with the leadership?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, right. I do apologise. Well, you know, this is a bit of a black comedy, really, because all of us, all of the signatories were supposed to go up there, and we set off on a road across Tvrdimici, and we wanted to go to this hotel at Jahorina and for the 18 of us to coordinate things because we met with the leadership at Kikinda. But there were 15 of us going to Lukavica and about about 7 or 8 of us only managed to get to Jahorina because we managed to leave about 12 people along the way. They gave up or something. So when we got there, there were only about 7 to 8 of us. And as a sign of support for what we had to say, the representative of Ilidza, Nedeljko Prstojevic, came along, as well. Even though we had not invited him originally, he somehow showed up and wanted to lend his support to our request even though he was not present at the original meeting. And so we had a stiff drink when we got there to give ourselves courage. So we went to where the Presidency was, and then on the way to Kikinda we managed to lose four or five extra people. And so when we finally got to our final destination, it was only myself, Mr. Prijic, Mr. Nedeljko Prstojevic, and, I think, Danilo Skrba. And so the four of us were the only ones out of these people who actually attended that meeting; whereas, as I said, we somehow lost the other people along the way. They wandered off, in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that a number of people dropped out of the group because they were scared of the possible consequences. What consequences were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is guesswork, of course, but there was war, and human lives were not worth all that much. And if at such times you voice criticism of certain things, especially your leadership, you can expect all sorts of consequences. I can't really guess exactly what consequences those could have been, but I must be honest and open here. When we arrived at that meeting, there were Mr. Krajisnik, Karadzic in that meeting room, and I was rather surprised by the fact that there were quite a few representatives of the armed forces there, as well; Mladic, Gvero, Tolimir. So those three top military commanders were there, and I was rather taken aback by that. I mean, what were they doing at that meeting since we were mostly addressing Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, and Koljevic? And as to the meeting itself, Karadzic didn't say much. He basically stayed silent throughout. Krajisnik did speak, and he tried to defuse the tension and make sure that we could talk freely and -- but we were frightened by Mladic, in fact. That was the problem, especially because Prijic engaged in direct verbal conflict with Mladic, and so we were really afraid for our lives because of Prijic's outright attack and -- at Mladic. He actually hurled an insult at him, and he was not very pleased. And so we in the end were quite pleased to have escaped safe and sound because we were very frightened of Mladic. He was very angry, arrogant, and unpredictable, and there was no way of talking to him normally or properly. And we had not been expecting him to attend that meeting. We did not know he would be there. We were expecting to see Krajisnik, Karadzic, Plavsic, and Koljevic. And for the most part, we talked to Krajisnik whilst Prijic was arguing with Mladic, and in the end he offended him in a big way, and we were pleased to have escaped unscathed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Neskovic -- oh, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that at that time there was a state of war and that human life did not have much value, and you said that when one allowed oneself to criticise the leadership, one could expect to suffer all sorts of consequences. Are there any examples you could provide us with, examples of certain individuals having suffered serious consequences at the time? Were any individuals killed? Were they threatened or obliged to flee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could only provide you with the example of Professor Mucibabic, who fled from the area. As for whether someone could have been killed for such matters, I know nothing about that. You know, when there is a state of war, if someone acted in such a manner, it wouldn't be done publicly, transparently. So I have no knowledge about such matters. But to be quite frank, I must say that we were very afraid of Mladic. But I think that Krajisnik managed to calm the situation down a bit, and it was possible to discuss matters. Krajisnik was very skilful when it came to engaging in discussions of various kinds. Momo Mandic told me that everything was fine, but he advised me not to come to Pale very frequently after that meeting because you had to pass through a forest. He said I should remain down in Grbavica. He said that I should not go on any particular trips for security reasons. I am sorry, I can't really answer that question because I'm not familiar with any such events. I couldn't provide you with the sort of example you've been referring to. All I know is that Professor Mucibabic fled; they criticised him for some reasons, and he quite simply fled and never returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question for you, as well: Could you briefly tell us what exactly the subject was or the subjects on which Prijic and Mladic had a clash during that meeting. What was the position of Mladic? Could you tell us a bit more about that clash.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were sitting very close to each other, and Mladic asked Prijic, who was a pharmaceutical expert, what he thought about the Serbian officers, and Prijic said -- or asked him whether he was referring to high-ranking officers or low-ranking officers. And then Mladic said that, of course, he was thinking of high-ranking officers. And then Prijic said that he believed that they were all thieves, cowards, and incompetent individuals. Mladic became very angry, and his face started changing colours, first red and then white, et cetera. And then Mladic asked him what percentage of officers were such as he had described them, and Prijic then said that he thought 90 per cent of the officers were as he had described them. And that is the kind of exchange they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no conflict on any operational matters, military operational matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. They only discussed the quality of the officers, and Prijic said that he believed that they were thieves, cowards, that they were incompetent, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the issue of Sarajevo and what might happen to it. Were you familiar at that time with the strategic objectives adopted at the May 12th, 1992, session of the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately because that Assembly session took place in Banja Luka, but we did find out that that was a strategic objective, but that objective meant nothing to the inhabitants of Sarajevo. We didn't know what that meant; if it meant that a Serbian Sarajevo had to be established, we weren't sure what that involved exactly. And secondly, the Assembly didn't say whether the Serbian and Muslim Sarajevo would, in fact, be a Serbian and Muslim municipality, and then at the level of the municipalities there would be a joint town administration, or perhaps they had imagined division of the town along the lines of the Berlin division. But independently of that strategic objective mentioned in Banja Luka, we constantly received information from various circles, from Serbian circles, from Bosniak circles, according to which they had already decided on a plan for Sarajevo and according to which Sarajevo would go to the Bosniaks. And this made everyone worried. And in addition, the entire leadership of Republika Srpska was said to have quite simply fled, and that included people living in Grbavica, such as Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic. Even they did not remain there; they fled. So the fact that the leadership fled to Pale, well, this made people think that the Serbs in Sarajevo would be traded at some sort of high international level, and we were particularly afraid of Milosevic. We were afraid that Milosevic might negotiate on behalf of the Serbs because he didn't know anything about Sarajevo, so we were afraid that he might engage in some sort of flippant trade with Sarajevo. So a lot of rumours were spread, and unfortunately after the Dayton Agreement what I have just been referring to was, in fact, confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you discussed a telephone conversation between, I believe, Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Djurovic during which Dr. Karadzic spoke about "their settlements" and about "our territory" and about "everyone on their land." And in that connection -- and that was in regards to Sarajevo, if you recall. In that connection, could I ask you to turn next to tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd ask that that be marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P914.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, P914 is a transcript of a film shot in 1992, entitled "Serbian epics." I'd like to direct your attention first to page 5 of the English translation and to a portion which appears -- if you'll see to the left, there are time indications for that film. On page 4 of the English version, there's a time indication of 26.35. And the first portion of the transcript to which I want to direct your attention appears six entries after that and after the Gusolj [phoen] player sings a song about the fair Turkish daughter and about -- and about the Serbs surrounding Sarajevo. Do you see that portion wherein Dr. Karadzic speaks?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me just find the Serbian translation so that I can find my bearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the page, last three digits at the top, 852, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there Dr. Karadzic states, "We must prove to the international factor that we are, in fact, not -- that we hold no siege over Sarajevo. Basically we are protecting our territories, and here it is visible that Sarajevo sprung up in Serbian territory, as Serbian property, and the entire surrounding of Sarajevo is Serbian. These are all Serbian villages, Serbian towns, Serbian settlements. We would not solve those issues," et cetera. And the next portion of the transcript to which I want to direct your attention appears at page 8 of the English translation. It's in a portion where Dr. Karadzic is speaking to Eduard Limonov.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the number at the top? I do apologise, but perhaps you could help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that would be -- just double-checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Limonov" appears in English on the top of page, last three digits, 856.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The English version I'm look at, the last three digits would be 859, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we see at 859 "Limonov" just a bit below the middle of the page, to say "its mighty weapon," which appears --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to help to direct the witness to the Serbian version of the transcript because I believe that Dr. Karadzic is speaking in English during this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So perhaps it's best if I just read that portion and it's translated to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sure. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The portion of the transcript which appears and I'm directing your attention appears at page 8, and it is as follows: "The Turks and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even Muslims who have" -- sorry. I'll start again. "The Turks and even Muslims who have been previously Serbs and converted into Islam, they used to live in centres of cities while Serbs used to possess the entire ground, and that was Serbian country." And the transcript indicates Dr. Karadzic is pointing towards Sarajevo. "When Turks came, we may be negotiating about territory, but we own this country. This is our country. Turks have been here occupiers, and the Muslims are successors of those occupiers." And then he goes on to point out the mosques. Mr. Neskovic, did Dr. Karadzic consider that Sarajevo was essentially Serbian land and Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that Mr. Karadzic expressed his position in politically incorrect terms. He had lived in Sarajevo for a long time, and he should have known where people had land. Most of the land in Sarajevo was state land. Then there was Muslim land, Serbian land, Jewish land. In the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, there was a lot of Croatian land. And this was the case at the time of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. After the Communist revolution, all of this land that had previously been private property was nationalalised, and it became state land. So to say that Sarajevo is Muslim or Croatian or only Serbian, well, this is just foolish. It's stupid, and it's not supported by the facts. There was privately owned land that belonged to all three ethnic groups, and there were a lot of buildings in the town that were owned by all three ethnic groups. So this is quite simply incorrect. And Karadzic, as an intellectual who lived in Sarajevo, could have been aware of these facts. I think that he expressed such positions for political reasons and probably in order to leave an impression on Limonov. I don't know what his reasons were, but what Karadzic said has nothing to do with the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note the time. I don't want to extend it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. We'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One housekeeping matter before we begin. I believe that a document -- or Exhibit 914 needs to be renumbered to encompass both the transcripts and the video itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be P914, and the transcript, P914A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I have relatively few remaining questions, and they'll be largely focussed on events in Novo Sarajevo. Let me ask you first whether in 1992 and more specifically the second half of 1992, let's say beginning in May and June, Muslims began to leave Novo Sarajevo in significant numbers.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, initially they wanted to live there. They didn't want to leave the territory of the municipality. As far as relationships with the Serbs are concerned, well, the Muslims and Croats were on very good terms. Initially the situation was fairly good, given the wartime conditions. But sometime in the second half of 1992 - perhaps that was in July or in August - certain groups started to expel the Muslims and made them flee to the other side of Miljacka. In Grbavica, there -- we have to distinguish between Grbavica I, where our Crisis Staff was located and where the civilian authorities were located, and there was also Grbavica II, which resembled Stalingrad; it was a military position. The situation was far more difficult. And I think that the Muslims were expelled in droves from Grbavica II. They were expelled over the bridge, and I'm not sure whether some sort of a 3rd Battalion was involved whose commander was Degbanovic [phoen] and whose nickname was Balija, but there were various bandits, individual bandits, or illegal groups who committed crimes, engaged in looting and maltreating of individuals. There was someone called Vlahovic, whose nickname was Batko, who was one such person. And then after Grbavica II, there was a critical day in Grbavica I, too. I can't remember whether it was in August 1992 or perhaps around that time. But on that occasion, one group of men in uniforms - I don't know who they were; I didn't try to obtain such information - but this group expelled some of the Muslims from their homes and made them cross over to the other side. Olja Varagic then came to see me. She had found out about some sort of a plan being prepared. I wasn't aware of that. She asked me whether I could help her; I said yes. I said, "This is what we'll do. I said, I'll go and see you in your flat." Orhan Dzipa, my colleague from Serbian Radio Television was already there in the flat. There were a lot of Muslims in the flat from the building, and they had a plan. If an armed group came to the flat, the plan was for me to appear at the door and say, "I'm a Serb. I live in this flat; don't come in", and so on and so forth. I don't know whether that would have worked or not, but fortunately no one came to that flat. So around August one could say that the expulsion of Muslims was being conducted on a larger scale. Before August there were individual cases of these people being expelled, but there were also certain requests from Muslim groups. They themselves said they wanted to cross over to the other side because they didn't feel safe there. And then there were many secret exchanges. Muslims from Grbavica went to the other side, and Serbs from Sarajevo came to this side. And criminal groups were involved in these activities, groups who do not have much respect for the law, because in the course of the war this cooperation never ceased. So the population was exchanged in this way, too. I spoke to certain people who wanted to leave at any cost. You know, people from Sarajevo, the Serbs and the Muslims, they were quite prepared to put up with hunger, with poverty, with the risk of war, et cetera, but they were not prepared to put up with being humiliated. A neighbour of mine -- a Muslim neighbour of mine said, "I will have to do something. I'll have to take a spade and dig trenches or work for the public utilities company. I can accept all of this, but I won't accept to be made to sing Chetnik songs." And he said, "That's why I would like to cross over to the other side." And then I contacted the chief of the police, Sipcic Simo, and Simo Sipcic helped him to cross over to the other side. Simo Sipcic could do that because his relative was the commander of a corps, Tomo Sipcic. They were relatives, so he could help. So in the first half of 1992, there were such individual cases. In the second half, expulsion was conducted on a large scale. As far as Grbavica I is concerned, as far as I can remember, this did not go on for days and days. I believe that this only occurred on one day, but it was a terrible day, an ugly day, and these very ugly things happened. On that day, individuals were expelled and made to cross over to the other side; this was quite unnecessary. I must emphasise that war was slow to break out in that urban area, and the Muslims in Grbavica acted in a very correct manner in relation to the Serbian army. But, on the other hand, there was a commander, major, called Dragan Petkovic. He also treated them very correctly because he lived there. So in April and May, the relationship was very good, given the wartime conditions. And I regret the fact that this relationship was not maintained. That is all I would have to say in response to your question for the time being. If you have any other questions you want to put to me, I can deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for clarification, when you said that Grbavica II resembled -- did you say Stalingrad, or did you say Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I mentioned Grbavica II, and I said it resembled Stalingrad, that armed combat was terrible. There was a lot of sniper fire, and it really resembled Stalingrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you mentioned someone named Batko. First of all, do you know whether he -- he held any official position within the military police or any other body?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was an armed monster, a pathological type. He wore an army uniform and nothing more than that. And I don't know whether he was a member of a paramilitary unit or a regular army unit; I really don't know. I don't know what the make-up of those military formations were. But he did a lot of bad things there. Because with mutual efforts on the part of both Serbs and Muslims, we managed to more or less strike a balance, and then an individual like that comes along and acts like a monster, and he spoils everything. And I mean, during the day, there were police officers there, and later on we had the French army there, and the security situation was rather good. But at night we had a problem because there was no lighting; there was no electricity; it's a big town, and the front lines were crossing across town. And so he, either on his own or with some of his partners in crime, would enter people's flats at night, and he stole property and was guilty of other misdeeds. There were even rumours about certain killings and murders. I've only heard it secondhand, as it were. I did not witness any of that myself. So whenever you crossed him in the streets, you didn't know whether he was going to say hello to you or he was going to shoot you. And, secondly, if he wanted to take anyone in -- the person didn't really have time to stay alive. He would never take a prisoner for one, two, or three days. In order for anyone to have a chance to have saving that person, it was a matter of minutes. Once he took my friend, Orhan Dzipa, and his dog, and Olja Varagic came to me and she said, "Let's try and save him," and I said, "I don't dare go there because he's going to kill me, as well." And we went to Simo Sipcic, who was the head of the police at the time, and then he ran to some -- Batko's rooms, and he saved Orhan Dzipa and the dog. So Simo could interfere -- or rather, could intervene with his cousin that this person should be taken away or imprisoned or sent away. And we wanted to free Grbavica from this guy, but then somehow after two or three weeks he would always come back. He kept coming back, and then we would once again ask for this person to be removed. And then he would be removed and then sent back again. And then we were even more frightened because we thought that perhaps he was not an isolated case, this Batko, and that he probably had some protection, and we didn't know what the matter was because he kept coming back and terrorised the population. I think even Biljana Plavsic intervened once and asked for him to be removed from the area once, and then he kept being removed and sent back. And I still don't know who he belonged to, what group of people he belonged to. Very sad things used to happen. I mean, we even had a marketplace organised during the war. The farmers would bring their produce to the market, and so the inhabitants would be able to buy stuff. But whenever he came along, everybody would flee, the sellers and the buyers, and the marketplace would be totally empty, and then he just helped himself to whatever he wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Your speed of speech is such that it's difficult for the transcribers and the interpreters to follow you. Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described everyone's fear and quite a number of incidents. Did everybody in the area know about this guy?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody knew of him. The military police knew of him; the civilian police knew and the military, as well. He was not an unknown phenomenon, as it were. He did whatever he did very openly. Don't misunderstand me. I mean, he never used to hide what he was up to or his misdeeds. So he was well known down there, and everybody tried to not -- not to cross paths with him, especially Muslims and Croats, but Serbs didn't like to be around him either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it understood that the primary targets of his attacks were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, yes, but the main targets of his attacks always had to do with money and looting, and then, of course, especially Muslims and Croats. Mostly Muslims, or in case he perhaps heard that there was some slightly better-off family and he supposed there might be money there. But he was involved in all sorts of violence, violence against women, men, looting, stealing, all kinds of violence, as I said. He was prone to violence, and the only thing that is unclear to me is once he was taken away, why was it made possible for him to come back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that he wore a uniform but you weren't certain whether he belonged to a paramilitary group or military group. If I could ask you a question about something you said during your April 2004 interview. At -- at that time, you were talking about Batko again. And you said at the bottom of page 126, "It was still the responsibility of the military police and army organs. Batko was a soldier, their member with their uniform and gun, and it was their duty, too." Do you recall now whether -- the kind of uniform Batko wore and whether he was -- whether he was considered to be a member of the -- the military police or army?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a military uniform. There were all sorts of uniforms at the time; I think it was a camouflage military uniform. And he sometimes wore a beret, and sometimes he didn't. But that was some kind of military uniform. He was not a member of the military police, though. And he combined those army fatigues with various other items of clothing, but there were no insignia denoting any ranks or anything. He was just an armed individual wearing a uniform without any other indication or any insignia on his uniform indicating that he was an officer or that he belonged to any particular unit. But as far as I'm aware of, he never took part in any real combat activity along the front lines, where real soldiers were, and he mostly acted in the background, behind the front lines, and did as he pleased. I do know -- well, there are not too many eyewitnesses, but there is general knowledge of the fact that he was responsible for the disappearance of a very respected gynaecologist, Miro Kundurevic, and I think he was guilty of violence against his wife, as well. Mrs. Kundurevic survived, and I think she is living abroad at the moment, and she is certainly going to be able to provide the full story of that because what I hear, what I know, is not firsthand knowledge; it's hearsay. But I think this lady, she knows everything, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question is about another subject, Your Honour, so if you want to continue with this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that period of time that you're referring to, sir, you were in a position of responsibility within the civilian government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe I should give you a really specific answer. I became president of the Crisis Staff at some point around the 10th of April, but this only referred to the area of Vrace because at that time for about a month the area of Grbavica was considered no man's land. It was not under the control of Serbs, not under the control of Muslims either. So the Crisis Staff between the period of time -- in the period of time between the 10th of April up until the 10th of May, roughly speaking, was active only at the local community of Vrace. And when Grbavica I was placed under the control of the Serb forces, well, at that stage the Crisis Staff was moved to the premises in that area. And as to Batko, straight away, at the very start, he was present in the area. But as to the crimes that he committed and with regard to Miro Kondurovic and others, I think that it happened slightly later. I think that it happened at some point in June, July, and so on because in April, whilst the conflict was going on, it was not an all-out war, in fact. People were going to work from Vrace and crossing over to the other side. And even my people used to cross over from one to the other side. So the war had not started as an all-out war as yet, and at around the time we went down to Grbavica, between May and June, as time went by, Batko himself stepped up his own activities, his own crimes, as it were. I was the president of the Crisis Staff up until the 5th of June, roughly speaking, and we did not hear any direct information about his crimes, but we did have complaints because Muslims were complaining about the fact that he was terrorising them, he was dangerous, and they were afraid of him, and the only thing I could do at the time was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Crisis Staff that you were presiding over, were there any representatives of the military authorities within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formally speaking, well, yes, we had the representative of the Territorial Defence, but his presence there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm talking about the army, about the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The armed forces, no. But prior to the creation of the armed forces, there was the Territorial Defence and the representatives of the Territorial Defence was there, and he kept asking for supplies, for money and wages for the soldiers, but there were no representatives of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you first of all kindly slow down because you are speaking very fast and it is difficult for the record. My question is the following: You are a man who is in a position of responsibility within the civilian authorities, as it were, and you had the opportunity to meet with the highest-ranking people within the hierarchy of that republic. Faced with actions such as the ones carried out by Batko, what was your reaction? Did you get in touch with somebody higher up? Did you alert people to what was going on? And when Batko was released after his initial detention, did you lodge a complaint? As a citizen, did you live up to your responsibilities, as it were? Because in a sentence earlier on in the course of your testimony - and I'm reading it now - you refer to crimes committed in Grbavica II and -- Grbavica I and II, and you're saying, "I can't really remember whether this was in August 1992, but on that occasion a group of uniformed men committed various crimes," and you go on to say, "A group of uniformed men - I don't know who they were - and also, I never tried to obtain any information to find out what they were." So what I'd like to know is why, when faced with so many crimes committed by Mr. Batko and faced with crimes committed by other people, as well, did you not reach any decisions in terms of alerting your authorities in order to ask them to put a stop to such a situation. That's my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply seek clarification before the witness deals with it. That passage, with respect, His Honour Judge Hanoteau has raised quite a number of questions, and I wonder whether it could be clear to me and perhaps the witness that -- is -- is, as stated, is Judge Hanoteau's question the very last question in those four or five lines, with everything else being some sort of introduction or preamble, or is the witness being asked to answer all or some of those questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is meant to answer this question; that is to say, how does he explain the fact that when faced with actions carried out by this gentleman, Batko, and others he did not decide to alert the highest civilian or military authorities, for that matter, especially considering that he had the possibility of contacting them on the basis of his position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to my own situation, I informed the chief of military police because I knew him in person. It was Mr. Sipcic. The higher ranking officials at Pale had not been informed. I did not inform them because I thought that it was up to the civilian police, the state security services, the military police, and the military structures and that it was up to them to solve the problem of Batko and all the other crimes in relation to that. I was of the view that the military structures and the police and especially the state security services were called upon to deal with this because this was within their area of competence, strictly speaking. As to my civic duty to raise the issue of Batko at the Crisis Staff or of opposing Batko openly, we did not dare do that because we would have lost our lives, quite simply, because apart from all the other obligations, we also had a duty to protect our own lives and those of our families. I did send a report to Pale, and I distanced myself from the military and the police, and I did indicate that I had nothing to do with them and that Radovan would have to look for and ask for a special report from the police and the armed forces. Why did I not do more as a simple citizen? Well, quite simply because I thought it was up to the regular police force and the regular military police and the state security services and the military unit that Batko belonged to. Obviously I disagreed with what Batko was doing. But had I been more open in my criticism or had I opposed him more openly, I would have put my life at risk. And also, you've heard the fact that the top leadership at Pale was told about Batko by Biljana Plavsic and it never yielded any results, and that meant that the civilian authorities were not in a position to prevent crimes unless they are in command of the military and police forces, as well. Had I been a commander that had the power or control over military and police units as the head of the Crisis Staff, in that case it would have been my direct responsibility, and in that case it would have been a question why I had not done something about it. But I was not the person who was in control of the police or the military, and I didn't even have any contact with them. And all the Crisis Staff could do was contact the police or the military. And the fact that I did not contact anyone at Pale, well, I found that it would have been totally useless. Why would I be the person to report that particular crime to the top leadership at Pale when it would have been more efficient on my part to get in touch with the chief of military police who was there on the spot, and so it was up to him to undertake certain measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said in your answer that you sent a report to Pale: "[In English] I distanced myself from the military Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the police, and I did indicate that I had nothing to do with them." [Interpretation] So you did send a report to Pale with regard to those incidents in which Batko was involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I submitted a report on the 5th of June. In that report, I did not actually make a specific reference to Batko himself. I did make a reference to certain looting, and I did stress that in as far as the police and military side of things is concerned, I had nothing to do with that, and I told the president that he should seek information from the military and the police on all those issues. Not because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting you, sir, but if you submitted a report to Pale with regard to theft of private property, can you tell me whether you also submit a report when murders took place against civilians. Did you sent a report to Pale about those killings? And I suppose you were a witness there, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not an eyewitness to those killings, and I did not send in a report on those killings because I felt that it was up to the police and the military, and we were a civilian body, a Crisis Staff, and we were not in control of the police. We were not higher up within the hierarchy in the area of Grbavica, so that's why I did not send in a report on killings. And, on the other hand, in order for me to be able to file a report on any killings at Pale, the police and the army would have had to send a detailed report to me beforehand; that is to say, what had happened, in what way, who exactly had been killed, who was guilty of those killings, and I would have had to have some initial information on which to base my report. But I never asked for this initial information, and I never got that information either from the police or the armed forces in order for me to be able to send a report to Pale. And let me reiterate once again. I felt that it was a legal obligation of the state security services, the civilian police, the military police, and the military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I actually wanted to ask you a question about the June 5th, 1992, report. And that can be found, if you recall, at tab 23. And specifically I'd like to address your -- I'd like to focus your attention on item 6, "Treatment of Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You find that at page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That states: "Citizens of all nationalities assemble frequently, especially in Grbavica, and our public attitude is very correct. We appoint a head of every building who is responsible for the situation in his building and for all the information about the occupants. Secretly, the police supply the usual procedure to people who were engaged in military activities against us." Now, first, where were the police operating who were responsible for Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, in the beginning of April, they were at Vrace at the local community premises. And when Grbavica was placed under the control of the Serb forces, they were at Zagrebacka Street, pretty close to the seat of the civilian authorities, in a kindergarten, and they were down there on the spot in the Zagrebacka Street. That was the police station for Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Mr. Mandic before. Were any of the high- ranking police officials or highest ranking police officials located in the general area of Novo Sarajevo? Either within the municipality or in the general area of where the police in Novo Sarajevo were operating.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the premises of the police academy at Vrace, also the entire ministry was there, and the Ministry of the Interior, Mico Stanisic, spent time there quite often. I don't know. There was a fence in there, and there were guards, so I don't know how often or for how long they were there. But it was at the police academy at Vrace, and that was where the MUP was operating. I don't know whether temporarily or for how long or whatever, but Mico Stanisic was there very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who Milenko Karisik was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that? Who did you understand him to be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a commander of the special police force, police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he also located in -- in your area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was there very briefly. I met him in the course of the fighting around the police academy at Vrace, and I really don't think he spent a long time there. At least, I'm not aware of that. Perhaps he might have been in the area on private business. But according to my recollection, he was there very briefly, and straight after the end of the combat activities, a couple of days later, I think, he left the area. But perhaps he visited occasionally. Maybe he went to Pale and then came back with Stanisic and then went back to Pale, but he was going back and forth between Pale and Vrace, and those people were there sometimes, and sometimes they were not. But I think that after the end of the combat operations around the academy, I think he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
