utterances.text: Now, the last sentence in the first paragraph of item 6 of the June 5th report, as I mentioned earlier, says, "Secretly, the police applied the usual procedure to people who were engaged in military activities against us." If you know, what was the usual -- what was the procedure that the police was applying to Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that since all the Muslims had been asked to surrender their weapons on a voluntary basis, and they did that, and Commander Major Petkovic said, "Since you have done that, the army won't search your flats. We'll have a Muslim at each entrance who will be in charge of that entrance and will ensure that everyone is there every night," and I think that we made some sort of a census there, listed the inhabitants who were there. This concerned Muslims who didn't want to surrender their weapons and they acted against the Army of Republika Srpska. They provoked action over the radio, or there was sniper fire because they believed that those who were carrying a weapon were no longer citizens; they were soldiers. And if any inhabitants noticed such a person, they should go to the civilian police and report on the fact, and then further police procedures would be implemented. So it meant that if anyone noticed such a person in their building, they should be reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that done secretly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, for the sake of the security of those who reported on these people, and if anyone acted against the Serbian army, they did so in secret, too, and the person who would report on them to the police would do that in secret, to conceal his or her identity and to -- to make sure that that person wouldn't suffer any consequences at a subsequent date. But it was their obligation to inform the civilian police if such information came to light. And then the civilian police would have to arrest the individual concerned, and that individual would then be subjected to the appropriate police procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. If I could have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neskovic. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before I give an opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, I would have, since we have this document in front of us, have one additional question to the witness. Mr. Neskovic, under paragraph 8 of your report, it reads, "Accommodation of fight fighters from other areas." And then "for those fighters from other areas we provide accommodation." What kind of fighters you were referring to when you drafted this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was thinking of people who had come from the other side of Miljacka, from the other part of the town that was under Muslim control. And then I had in mind combatants who later left the area of Popalici, when the Popalici also fell into the hands of the Muslim army. So the reference is to fighters from Sarajevo who were not from Grbavica. They either came from other local communes, Popalici, Velesici, central parts of town, or they came from some of the surrounding villages. On the whole, the reference is to local Serbian fighters. As far as I know, at the time there were no foreigners among them, and some of the Muslims, especially in Vrace, left a certain residential area on a voluntary basis, and occasionally we'd provide accommodation for those combatants. Some had flats that were available. We didn't provide them with permanent accommodation. And in some way, they kept these flats. If the flats hadn't been used, they would have been looted or damaged. So I think that what we did was useful. We managed to protect those flats and provide these people with accommodation. There were a lot of people from the Muslim side who were either exchanged or released or they were released in exchange for money or they fled, et cetera, but our front lines were sometimes 5 metres away, 10 metres away, sometimes 25 metres away. There was one front line that was only 50 centimetres away; there was just a wall there. And those are the combatants referred to. They usually were provided with accommodation in the Vrace area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You've answered my question. The details of the confrontation lines are not vital for it. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just recover the -- the lectern. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, you'll now be examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you -- you signed your membership card and joined up to the SDS, you told the Trial Chamber, on the 12th of July, 1990. Can you say in brief terms what it was that encouraged or inspired you to join the SDS at that point.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was a member of another party, called the Democratic Party of Freedom, which was registered in Mostar. The SDS was formed by assembling seven or eight minor parties and groups, and the representative of our party, Mrs. Bozana Radovic, established contact with Karadzic in the Democratic Party of Freedom. We weren't aware of this, and she decided to join our party to the SDS. She decided that our party should join the SDS. We had certain problems, and then on the 11th of July, just before the SDS was established, Radovan came and -- to the Holiday Inn. He visited all the various -- or he spoke to all the various party leaders and asked whether they wanted to join in. I was the representative of the Democratic Party of Freedom, and it was at that session that the SDS was joined. I signed a membership card for that party. And what was the reason for doing that? Well, you know, there was not really any other party you could join. There was the SDA, the Muslim party; there was the Croatian party, the HDZ; then you had Anto Markovic's party, and the SDP party, and these parties were falling apart. So as a Serb, it was quite normal for me to join that party, especially since the term "democratic" was included in the title of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your own inclination coincided with the fact that your existing party was joining up with the SDS, so, in a nutshell, it was just really the obvious place for you to go at that time, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been politically active beyond membership of a political party over the period up to July 1990?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not held any offices or working positions in any political party; is that -- is that the position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree, that is the position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unless we mention the fact that I was somewhat involved in the Democratic Party of Freedom with certain individuals, but I didn't really have any particular duties. Up until July, I didn't have any political party duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any formal position in that Democratic Party of Freedom, or had you had at any time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was some kind of a vice-president there, and Mr. Djukic from Sokolac was the president, and we remained at the level of a committee. We'd been registered. We wanted a founding Assembly in Sarajevo, in Skenderija, but given -- given the fact that not many citizens responded, this fell through. But we were a minor party that had been duly registered. I think that Djukic was at the head of the party, Djukic from Sokolac. I've forgotten his name. Bozo Radic from Nevesinje was a prominent member; then there was Goran Milic, who is now some sort of BH diplomat, and there were several other individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, probably it will help to proceed a bit quicker if you try to resist the temptation to give a lot of more detailed information in addition to the answer to the question and see what further questions come along. Mr. Neskovic, when you say you were some kind of a vice- president, that simply means you were a vice-president, full stop, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was the vice-president of that party, but at the founding session, when a president and vice-president were to be officially elected, well, this did not occur because the Assembly fell through, and that is why the party then joined the Serbian Democratic Party because it was quite obvious that it could not be established on an independent basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get it clear, Mr. Neskovic. Whatever -- so whatever deficiencies there might have been in the formalities, in fact, you had been the vice-president, as opposed to one of a number of vice- presidents -- you had been the vice-president of that previous party, the Democratic Party of Freedom.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; although, that party wasn't really active. It hadn't even made any public announcements. It had only just been registered, and it was only going through -- it was only in its -- it was only starting out. So, in fact, it wasn't really known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's -- let's move on, Mr. Neskovic. You -- you made a speech at Pale on the 10th of August, 1990, and that was actually in, among others, Dr. Karadzic's presence, wasn't it, when you made that speech; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make that speech in any official capacity or just as a speaker from the floor at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a speech on behalf of the Municipal Committee of the Serbian Democratic Party in Pale. A day before, I went to a meeting of that Municipal Committee, and it wasn't my intention to give a speech, but they asked me whether I had any ideas as to what should be done on the following day. I made a few suggestions. They then said, "Well, those suggestions aren't bad. Would you like to give that speech," which I did. There were other individuals who gave speeches, and that occurred on the 10th of August at the football stadium in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is -- is this what happened, Mr. Neskovic: Your -- your local colleagues thought it would be a good idea if you made a speech setting out these points, and then Dr. Karadzic liked what he heard from you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether Karadzic liked what he heard or not, but what you've just said is correct. My local colleagues thought it would be very useful if I gave a speech, which I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic heard what you said and then very shortly afterwards approached you to invite you to take an active role in the SDS, didn't he? That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Neskovic, can we agree Dr. Karadzic plainly must have liked at least something of what you said? That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic didn't approach me for the speech. He approached me for different reasons, because of the profession that I had, because of the job I had in the radio and television company in Sarajevo. I was well acquainted with election campaigns and with elections, and those are the reasons for which he approached me. It wasn't because of my speech. My speech was given in the way that other people gave speeches; my speech resembled the speeches that other people made. Dr. Karadzic approached me because he thought I was someone who could help with the election campaign since, given his profession, he knew very little about such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- what you had said -- this is at page 12 of yesterday's transcript, at line 3 -- was that -- "But after my speech at Pale on the 10th of August, Radovan did ask me whether I would like to take on analytical tasks within the SDS." Now, did Dr. Karadzic himself suggest what those analytical tasks should be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned analytical tasks that had to do with analysing the statute of municipalities, analytical tasks that had to do with changing the laws, analytical tasks that had to do with all the factors that influence an election. He also referred to the analysis of the media. An overall analysis was concerned as far as the elections are concerned. This is what he said, and I then accepted this task. It was interesting for me; it was a challenge. It was something that I was professionally interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Dr. Karadzic make it clear to you, then, on the occasion of that speech and meeting on the 10th of August that your responsibilities would involve your attending meetings of the Main Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't assign such a task to me, but he put me on the list of the Main Board, not as a member but as someone who should attend the sessions of the Main Board, which were held in the Hotel Serbia in Ilidza. I attended these sessions, and I actively participated in the discussions at those meetings of the Main Board. These discussions had to do with the election campaign, as this was the main subject of discussion at all these sessions. I was very active, and I attended those meetings regularly, and I did the job I had or I carried out the task I had been assigned to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it -- did your attendance at meetings of the Main Board start pretty much straight away after the invitation by Dr. Karadzic for you to become actively involved?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any -- any note or record whatever of your speech that you gave on the 10th of August, 1990, in Pale?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I can say is that I remember parts of the speech that I gave. I'm not sure whether anyone else has a written record of my speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- was the meeting at which you gave the speech open to the press?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a meeting in the open, at the football stadium. It was quite open, and anyone could have attended it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was any newspaper report of what you said?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I think the newspaper reports stated that a Municipal Assembly was held on such-and-such a day in Pale because there were many such Assembly sessions that were held during that period. In two or three months, there were almost 70 or 80 boards that had been established. So you would receive information on a daily basis about the establishment of such boards. Usually the press would report on Karadzic's speeches, as he was a more prominent figure; whereas, the speeches given by other individuals were not really something that the press was interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your visits - and you've described those in your evidence, particularly - don't worry about this reference -- page reference yourself, Mr. Neskovic. It's page 19 of yesterday's transcript. But did your visits to municipal meetings begin at some time after you were elected as deputy chairman of the Executive Committee at the end of July 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to interrupt. I just need to note that for some reason we have different pagination on -- I'll just need a little bit more guidance when there's reference to the page numbers or a little more time to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, well -- yes, of course. Could -- I'm, of course, more than happy to do that. I'm familiar with this problem. Could I have a clue as to what the discrepancy or disparity is, and then I might be able to help more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, on the -- on the other reference, the first reference you made - I think it was page 12, line 3 - it shows up on my transcript or it showed up on my transcript at page 11, approximately line 18. So there was that difference in the early portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see. And then -- and then page -- I've got page 19, line 3, a reference to -- or line 2: "I attended a number of municipal meetings all over the place." It sounds as if that might be at page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With that kind of help I'll be able to find it. I just wanted to ask for that early. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try and give a clue as to a phrase or something like that that will pick out the passage, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Neskovic, apologies. We sometimes do need to sort those things out. You were -- just to recap on that, you were, you said, elected as deputy chairman of the Executive Committee of the SDS on the 31st of July, 1991. My question was, Did your visits, as you've described them, to municipality meetings begin sometime after that? I think that's a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Far earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Then when did -- and I'm talking about, just to give you some sort of factual reference point -- you said - and this is page 19 of my transcript, line 1 - it's probably a few lines earlier in a - - it's in a 12-line answer from you, Mr. Neskovic. You said, "I was a kind Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of party activist who travelled around trying to solve organisational or staff issues in various municipalities. I attended a number of municipal meetings all over the place, so I was a party activist." And just as an introduction to this question, what you were talking about there was how in 1993 you had really picked up the same job you'd had, you said, in 1991. So the question is, That sort of activity that you describe, going round to municipal meetings all over the place, when did that start?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two types of activities. What you have just mentioned took place after the 12th of July, but before that date I also travelled around and was involved in Municipal Boards of the SDS, but I was involved in other activities. I was involved in the elections in the SDS because the Serbian Democratic Party from spring 1991 until July 1991 had elections in the party and it was being reformed. There were local boards that were becoming the basic boards, so I spent that period working on elections in that party. When the elections were completed, I continued working as a -- a member and vice-president of the Executive Board, and I attended meetings and dealt with regular party issues. Unfortunately, the main subject was the clash of fractions, and I spent most of my time dealing with these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I'll be permitted this comment. At page 12 of the transcript yesterday, we've got the 12th of July cropping up as a date, both in 1990 and 1991, and we also have some confusion between 12th of June and 12th of July. So it's just that these - - that particular date, it requires to be approached with some degree of -- of care and caution, which is why I'm going very specifically here with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, please, with -- avoiding any confusion as far as you can or ambiguity about which year, could I invite you to be as specific as you possibly can be about when you began to make these visits to municipalities around Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but the electoral activities, with the aim of organising the elections, went on between March and the 12th of July when the electoral Assembly took place. After the 12th of July, after that Assembly, a couple of days later, the Executive Committee was appointed, and then I continued to visit municipalities as a member of that Executive Committee, after the 12th of July, and all the way up until perhaps the end of that year. I can't be really specific; this is a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, it seems, first of all, clear now that because of your reference to elections that those dates you've just been referring to are clearly 1991. We -- we agree about that, do we?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that you referred to "I continued to visit municipalities as a member of the Executive Committee," and I -- my previous question was specifically concerned to know when those visits began. So did you make such visits with any sort of regularity or frequency -- did you make such visits earlier than the period of electoral reforms and activities that began in March 1991? Did you -- I'll shorten that question, make it very simple, Mr. Neskovic: Did your visits to the various municipalities, as you've described them, did they begin earlier than March 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, prior to March 1991 I visited perhaps two municipalities. And on the 11th of August, I was at the founding meeting for the setting-up of the SDS in Sokolac, and I went to Rogatica for the same reason. And I can't remember anything else really, if I went anywhere else. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that 11th of August you're talking about is the 11th of August, 1990, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your task of visiting municipalities a development of the analytical work for which you had first been brought in, or was it a separate job that you were given within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a separate job. At Sokolac, I was present as a delegate from Pale to give a speech; I was a visiting speaker there. And as to Rogatica, I was there together with other SDS leaders. I think Danilo Veselinovic was there and somebody else, probably. And we witnessed the founding of the Municipal Board of the SDS. So it was a different role, nothing to do with analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take the date that you were elected as the deputy chairman of the Executive Committee of the SDS. So that's the very end of July 1991, the 31st of July. Up to that date, can you say, as accurately as you can manage -- can you say how many visits you had made for the SDS to other municipalities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm really unable to answer that question. I never recorded it all, and I just can't remember. I don't want to guess. But I visited municipalities if there was need for me to do so. I did not visit them as a tourist. I would go if there was a problem, but unfortunately I really don't know. I've forgot, and I haven't recorded all those occasions, and I can't give you a specific number of times after 14 years. I believe that we are talking about the period of time between July 1991 onwards, and I think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Neskovic, please listen more carefully to my question. That is precisely not the period I was asking you about. You've just said, "We're talking about the period between July 1991 onwards." I had specifically asked you about the period up to the end of July 1991. So, Mr. Neskovic, with the greatest respect, please concentrate very specifically on what I'm asking you. So I'm going to put it again, then, and invite you to just give the best estimate you can, if you can, from your recollection. How many visits to other municipalities in Bosnia had you made by the time you were appointed deputy chairman of the Executive Board on the 31st of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I visited quite a few municipalities. There were only very few left that I had not visited. I think the only ones I had not visited were in Herzegovina. And as to all the other municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I visited them and some of them on many occasions. So there were quite a few visits. It would probably be easier for me to tell you where I did not go rather than where I did go because I went to quite a few places throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I never went down to Herzegovina, Foca, Gorazde, and Herzegovina; those were the only places I did not go to. And as to all the other areas -- but no, I didn't go to Western Herzegovina, either. But I went everywhere else, and I visited almost every single place, and some of the places I visited several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, let's just deal first of all with some very simple numbers, then. First of all, maybe I've got this wrong. Were there -- were there 109 municipalities at that time, or was it some different number?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 109, with Neum, but I think in about 10 to 15 municipalities there was no SDS organisation, such as Western Herzegovina. There was nothing -- there were no Serbs there, so there wasn't any possibility to organise that. But I believe that in the majority of municipalities, 80 or more, SDS had an organised party structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, again, just some -- perhaps we're coming to a break, but just some very simple ground rules, if I may respectfully suggest them. I -- that question simply asked you for agreement or correction as to the number of municipalities. That was all I had asked you. So if you agreed with my number, all you had to do, please, was say you agreed, and then we could have moved on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient point to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it at least is a convenient moment to interrupt the examination of the witness. I have to deal with a few procedural matters, which takes us another five minutes, but the witness can leave the courtroom and is expected to be back at five minutes to 1.00. So you can escort the witness out of the courtroom, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to give two decisions. The first decision is a decision on admission of certain items into evidence. For various reasons in the course of the proceedings, these items have been admitted only provisionally, although no objection has been raised by the parties so far. Therefore, the Chamber admits all the following items into evidence as of tomorrow, unless last-minute objections are raised by either party within the next 24 hours. These items are: P292 - and there's a clarification. P292 is admitted without the comments of the witness recorded before the intercept tabs; then P573 to P574L, P575 up to and including P580; P742 up to and including P746; P392 up to and including P406; P763 up to and including 763.B; P764 up to and including 787, and P817 up to and including 826; P791 up to and including P800; P814 up to and including 816; P827 up to and including 846; P890 up to and including P892. I also confirm to the registrar that P220 was admitted into evidence on the 7th March of 2005. I refer to transcript page 10091 because there might be some confusion on the basis of that transcript. Yes, as it says here, "Although a problem with the transcript might have created misunderstanding on this." This concludes the Chamber's decision on admission of certain exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a handout is given to the parties which indicates clearly what is admitted public and what is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instead of reading all the numbers again, Madam Registrar is invited to file the handout just given to the parties, which clearly indicates what exhibits are admitted under seal and what exhibits are admitted as public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been extremely helpful to have been sent these electronically in the past, as well, which we have been. We'd be very grateful to -- to have that again on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record, Mr. Stewart. Then the next decision is a decision regarding the exhibits in relation to witness Nielsen. Mr. Nielsen's exhibits have been provisionally numbered, but not, as yet, admitted into evidence. The reason for the delay is that the Prosecution choose not to use all the tabs in the three presentation binders. Mr. Tieger has since met with the Defence and has given his reasons why the Prosecution wishes to retain in evidence 32 of the unused tabs. We were informed today that the Defence does not object to the admission of these items. To make matters more comprehensible, also in this respect we have prepared a handout, which I would now kindly ask Madam Registrar to distribute to the parties. As indicated in the handout, of the 78 tabs in the three binders of exhibits provisionally marked P763.C, a certain number of tabs were blank and a certain number of them were already in evidence. Mr. Tieger has indicated that the Prosecution is not seeking admission of the tabs shown under (d) - that's small (d) - in the handout. The Prosecution does, however, seek admission of the 32 items under (e) - that's small (e) - in the handout. The Chamber accepts that these items represent essential reference documents to understand Nielsen's testimony, or are summary diagrams, or are documents implicitly or explicitly referred to during the testimony of the witness, albeit not physically handled by the witness in court. In summary, the Chamber admits the following items into evidence: P763, this is the expert report. P763.1 is the B/C/S translation. P763.A, this is an addendum to the report. P763.B, this is Mr. Nielsen's CV. P763.C, this stands for the three presentation binders. The tabs to be admitted into evidence are shown in the handout accompanying this decision. The status of all the exhibits is public. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the matter of Mr. Nielsen's exhibits, and Madam Registrar is invited to file the handout so that we know exactly what tabs are in evidence and which tabs are not in evidence. This concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- just ask -- it's just a simple practical question. I had -- I had -- I had looked earlier today at an exchange of e-mails between Ms. Loukas and Mr. Tieger, and I noted that they had reached agreement in relation to these matters, and who would I be to interfere with such a happy situation, Your Honour. May I just ask -- Mr. Tieger probably can confirm -- that this handout, as far as he's concerned, it reflects and coincides with that agreement reached between Ms. Loukas and him in the e-mail; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have not checked the numbers specifically, but I understand that it's based on that e-mail, and my -- my cursory look at it at this point suggests that it certainly is consistent with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's quite enough for my purposes, Your Honour. I wasn't pinning Mr. Tieger to say he poured over it item by item. But if that's -- they're intended to coincide, that was my question. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed about the content of the e- mail, and the Chamber checked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I'm doubly grateful, Your Honour. That seems to deal with that completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I say "the Chamber," at least the legal staff of the Chamber checked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have a faint idea of how these things might work, Your Honour, yes, on that level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour. I won't take the Court's time. We had begun working out the process whereby the Prosecution would receive copies of any documents that Mr. Krajisnik wanted to use during his cross-examination. I have not received any for this witness, and I would ask for that or at least an opportunity to see any documents that he intends to use for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there are some documents provided by Mr. Krajisnik, and this also gives me an opportunity to -- where some of the exhibits that were not yet admitted were waiting for a further evaluation of the documents provided by Mr. Krajisnik, that the first matter on our programme is now to clearly identify what was presented, what was already in evidence, what was not in evidence, whether we have translations, so to go through all this material in detail so that finally proper decisions will be taken in respect of the admission into evidence of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we just ask that particular care is taken with line 8 of the transcript as it stands at the moment when it comes to be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was all, Your Honour. Your Honour, that was intended as a fairly light-hearted remark, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Perhaps I'm not light-hearted enough to immediately understand, Mr. Stewart. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you -- you made an offer which I'm not going to take up, which was to list the municipalities that you didn't visit during that period, but I am, then, in the light of that going to just press you to give your best estimate of the total number of municipalities that you did visit up to the 31st of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between March 1991 and the 31st of July, 1991, I would have had to visit at least something in the range of between 25 or 30 municipalities. I do apologise for a certain lack of precision. It is a bit difficult to give you a precise answer because there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, of course, I'm quite sure neither the Trial Chamber and certainly not I am asking you to say anything more than you actually remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said - and this is at page 60 and -- the top of page 61 today --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said at the top of page 61 today was that -- you said, "I think I visited quite a few municipalities. There were only very few left that I had not visited." Now, Mr. Neskovic -- Mr. Neskovic, the arithmetic doesn't really quite work there, of 109 municipalities and you say that you estimated -- that you visited something like 25. I'm just going to urge you, please, to try and be a -- as clear as you possibly can. Which is it? That you visited the vast majority of the municipalities or something like 25 or -- or what? Can we just be clear about what you do now remember about how many municipalities you visited during that period.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be easier for me to list them one after the other. That would jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm just slightly reluctant because of how long it might take to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, do you say you can just reel them off quickly for us in a matter of -- of three or four minutes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be quick. Novo Sarajevo, Sokolac, Pale, Rogatica, Konjic, Tuzla, Travnik, Busovaca, Brcko, Modrica, Obudovac, I think even Doboj, Derventa, Prijedor, Maglaj, Zenica. I think I went to Jajce, as well. And then there are several other municipalities that I visited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the -- was the pattern and frequency of visits to municipalities then similar from the 31st of July onwards to the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Up until the 31st of July, it had to do with the pre- electoral activity within municipal organisations, electoral matters. After the 31st of July, we are talking about other activities, routine work of Municipal Boards and their functioning and overcoming problems and disagreements between fractions within those Municipal Boards. So those are two different types of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it -- is it this, then, Mr. Neskovic: In the first phase, up to the 31st of July, it was to do with organisational and structural matters relating to elections?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second phase, after the end of July, it was troubleshooting or sorting out problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The functioning of those municipal organisations in line with the statute that was approved at the electoral Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was troubleshooting. You went to -- after the 31st of July, you -- you generally went to municipalities to sort out specific problems that had arisen in those municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they frequently infighting or personnel problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. There were ongoing conflicts amongst fractions because some members of SDS were in power and others were not, and there were differences along those lines and then also with regard to different settlements. For example, some area might have considered themselves to be neglected, and then there was lobbying and private interests and all sorts of things. But that was an enormous permanent characteristic within the SDS that people kept bickering all the time. There were conflicts and arguments all the time, and it was very exhausting, especially for me. Other people did not really deal with that or to a lesser extent, so I was the one who had to carry that burden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went often, did you, as some sort of conciliator or mediator?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to solve problems, to bring about reconciliation. Compromise was just one option. And if it was not possible, we would sometimes even dissolve those Municipal Boards and organise fresh elections. And another possibility was to de-legitimise both factions and look for a third option. Well, there were different ways of solving those problems. But it mostly depended on our own behaviour when we visited those municipalities. First of all, did we have good background information? Did we act respectfully, et cetera? For the most part, people in the field didn't want us to come along and issue orders and act like some kind of authority and preach to them because otherwise we would have been chased away. So we had to adopt an analytical, a serious approach, act in an objective and unbiassed way, and listen to the arguments put forward by both parties. So compromise was the most frequently adopted solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, I want to ask you about a particular point in your evidence yesterday, but I -- I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to have to give you quite a little bit of context as will become apparent, I think. Your Honour, this the whole passage begins at -- it's page 18 of my transcript. It's probably a little bit earlier in Mr. Tieger's. But there's an exchange, Mr. Tieger, Judge Orie, the registrar, Mr. Tieger, and then a question beginning "Mr. Neskovic, the document before you now, Prosecution 895." I hope that helps to -- I see that that has identified the passage. And then the document that was put was dated February 1993. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was then the next bit, where you say that in February 1993 you continued in the same job you'd had in 1991, and then you were going on to give that description of attending municipal meetings. So the reason I'm giving this introduction is because this whole passage involves some mixture of 1991 and 1993. You were asked, "Were you considered a de facto member of the Executive Board," and you said, in a nutshell, yes. And then you went on to deal with questions of commodities reserve. Them the question of Mr. Ostojic came up, and you were asked -- this is page 20 in my transcript, line 5: "Was Mr. Ostojic still the Minister of Information at that time?" You said, "I can't remember exactly. At the time, I think he was no longer information minister." Now, do you agree at this point, Mr. Neskovic, you're clearly talking about 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. February 1993, after the renewal of the party because between June 1992 and February 1993 the party had actually been banned, so it was newly set up in February 1993. And a new Executive Committee was selected with a new president, Jovo Mijatovic, and they were distributed various tasks. And I don't think that Mr. Mijatovic was a member of the government anymore because the journalists had signed a petition against him, so he was chased away from the government. And as to whether -- and as to whether Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, you really have to slow down because the interpreters cannot follow your speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I'll keep it in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just say, Mr. Neskovic, you're being doubly enthusiastic because you're, first of all, volunteering quite a bit beyond what I specifically asked you the question, and then in your enthusiasm, you're going at the high speed that His Honour mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you'd very much limit yourself to answering to the specific question of Mr. Stewart, this will also prevent you from getting at high speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Neskovic, you're talking about Mr. Ostojic. You agreed we're talking about 1993. And then you said, "Ostojic might have had a role because he was Minister of Information" -- it must be "in" the previous government. I'm filling in the word "in." "So he probably had some kind of link with the government." And then you went on -- and this, after all that, Mr. Neskovic, this is what I want to ask you about. You say, "It doesn't really make sense because all the liaising with the government went through Karadzic and Krajisnik as top officials." Now, first of all, in giving that bit of your answer there, about all the liaising with government going through Karadzic and Krajisnik, were you talking about 1993 or 1991 or both?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The liaison with the Republika Srpska government always went through Karadzic and Krajisnik, at all times, in all the relevant years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about 1992, as well, are you, there? Or let me rephrase it. Would --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that answer would apply -- in what you're saying, would apply to 1991, 1992, and 1993, would it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, then, liaising with the government; you are talking about -- perhaps you indicated this a moment ago. Please confirm. You're talking about the government of Republika Srpska, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I am also thinking about the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you've answered my next question --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which there were eight Serbian ministers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've answered my next question, Mr. Neskovic, so we can move on, then. Let's take first of all liaison with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then; let's take that first. If you're now talking about liaison with the Bosnia and Herzegovina government going through Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, what period do you mean there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the period from January 1991, when the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being established, and then right up to February -- or rather, December 1991, when a special Serbian ministerial council was founded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there you are meaning, are you, that high-level contacts between the Bosnian Serbs and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina went through Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the thrust of what you were saying about -- well, let's forget Mr. Ostojic. That's a different period. What -- what you are saying is that -- let's look at the period from the middle of 1991 onwards, Mr. Neskovic. The difficulties that faced Bosnia and Herzegovina and the difficulties that faced the Bosnian Serbs within Bosnia and Herzegovina were fundamental, big political issues involving the different nations within Bosnia, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent, I would say that that is correct, but to the -- to a certain extent, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's see what we can agree about. The second half of 1991 and into 1992 the big issue was what was going to be the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it? Whether it was going to remain part of -- of Yugoslavia or whether it was going to -- to go down the route of independence, following Croatia and Slovenia. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the crucial issue; what the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina was was the key issue. The status of the state was the main issue. But in addition to that, there was another problem. The party leaders and primarily Karadzic and Alija Izetbegovic in a certain sense transformed the political system in Bosnia and Herzegovina and made it a party state, so those fundamental state issues were not discussed that much in the official institutions of power. These issues were more discussed by party leaders, and there were many people in Bosnia and Herzegovina who expected a favourable outcome when these conversations were -- or discussions were conducted. I think the main problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the fact that constitutional issues were ignored and problems were not resolved in accordance with the Constitution and in accordance with international law. Problems were resolved through interparty agreements, which did not yield any results, which did not provide any solutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try and deal with this as quickly as we can, Mr. Neskovic. Such was the importance of these issues that their attempted resolution involved some very high-level players from the international community, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I was under the impression that all the powerful people in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and that includes Serbian, Croat, and Muslim individuals - my impression was that they were trying to create a situation on an independent basis -- they were trying to deal with the situation independently, and they weren't asking the international community to get involved, although it was quite clear that the issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its status as a state could not be dealt with without the international community becoming involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were particularly active on the part of the Bosnian Serbs during that period in dealing with the other party leaders, such as Mr. Izetbegovic and representatives of the international community, included, didn't they, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Dr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Biljana Plavsic and to a certain extent Aleksa Buha, Vojislav Maksimovic, and as I have said, there was Biljana Plavsic, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not yourself involved at all at all in that level of discussions, negotiations, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally attended one such meeting in the office of -- in Mr. Krajisnik's office. These were interparty discussions between the SDS and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. It was around 1991, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've never attended any meeting with any representative of the international community, did you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made your visits to the municipalities, as you've described, in 1991, you were not carrying to the municipality instructions from the leadership of the SDS, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't carrying any particular kind of instructions. The statute was quite sufficient for me, the statute that was in force. To be frank, I acted in a fairly independent manner. It was possible for me to decide on how to deal with certain problems; I could do this in an independent manner. But I had not been issued any precise tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever -- and let's -- we're talking about 1991 now, but any time, the whole of 1991 is covered by this question, Mr. Neskovic. Before you visited any municipality, did you ever sit down or discuss on the -- sit down with Mr. Krajisnik or have a telephone conversation with Mr. Krajisnik in which he gave you any sort of briefing in advance of that visit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, Krajisnik wasn't involved in those party activities. I would usually appear on my own, or I would discuss matters with Karadzic. But as far as my work is concerned, Krajisnik didn't get involved in the regular activities of the party. He was the president of the Assembly. He had a high-level position, and he and Karadzic were involved in far more serious matters. As far as I know, he did not meddle in the activities of the party itself; at least, he didn't meddle in party activities as far as my activities are concerned. I don't know if he got involved in any other activities, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever -- following a meeting to -- a visit to a municipality in 1991, did you ever meet Mr. Krajisnik or telephone him to give him any report back on that visit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have anything to do for him. I was a member of the Executive Committee; he was -- Krajisnik was a member of the Main Board. So I didn't have the responsibility of reporting to Mr. Krajisnik. I submitted reports to the Executive Board or to Karadzic himself; although, when I returned from the field, if I wanted to submit a report to Karadzic, I realised that he was already informed of what I had been involved in, even before I returned from the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the structure. This is at page 22 of -- of my version of the transcript, and it begins -- the answer -- it's quite a long answer from you, Mr. Neskovic, and it begins at the foot of page 21 of my transcript: "Well, if I may make a correction here." It follows a six- line question, and then the answer starts "Well, if I may make a correction here. According to the statute from 1991, the 12th of July." I think that identifies that passage. You then go on about 12 lines or 13 lines or so down: "And two key principles were decided upon on that occasion," which is 12th of -- sorry, I'm just trying to identify that occasion. 12th of July, 1991. I stand to be corrected because the 12th of July seems to, of course, keep coming up, perhaps not surprisingly. "The basic body" -- you said, "Two key principles were decided upon on that occasion, one of them being that the main structure or the basic body would be a local community or a local committee and not a municipal one. So they would start at the very lowest rung." And you said -- the next paragraph: "The basic structure or the basic part of the party structure was this local committee, so that was the most important body at the local level; whereas, the president" -- and you're talking about Dr. Karadzic there -- "had the most power at the global level." So that's the two ends of the chain, if you like. This was the basic structure, wasn't it, but -- from the bottom up. You get the local committees; then you've got the Municipal Board, and then in some cases there's a Regional Board. And then you move to the Main Board of the SDS, and then -- well, you've got the president of the party. That's -- that -- that's right, isn't it, that -- that brief summary, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to explain this. Party activities were organised in such a way that local boards formed its basis. As far as Dr. Karadzic is concerned, in accordance with the statute, he represented the organ of the party, and he had a lot of authority. There was the Main Board and the Executive Board, which was the Executive Board in relation to the Main Board. So Karadzic was someone who represented the organ of the party, but the local board is the main way in which the party would become involved and take action in the field. So I don't see any contradiction here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, in effect notionally I was, if you like, well, inviting you to just imagine you're drawing up a simple chart on a piece of paper. So at the bottom we've got the local committee; then above that you write in "Municipal Board"; and then above that in some parts of Bosnia you write in "Regional Board"; and above that you put "Main Board," with perhaps "Executive Committee" sort after alongside that. You're nodding. You seem to agree so far with that as a simple description of the structure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your municipality, how many of these local committees were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the number of local communes. These local SDS organisations would usually overlap with the territory of local communes. If we're referring to a town such as Sarajevo, Banja Luka, in which local communes were too large, then you might have a number of local committees. But the rule was that a local committee would have up to 15 members, and each member of the local committee would be active on behalf of about 20 households. So in a given territory, you could have one or several local committees. It depended on how densely inhabited these areas were. But in essence, these local communes existed to avoid the party from becoming too bureaucratic and from ensuring that party organs did not exert too much influence. To become a member of the Municipal Board, you had to pass through the local committee, and then on the basis of such activity, you would become a member of Municipal Boards. That concerned two-thirds. So this was a principle that existed to prevent the party from becoming too bureaucratic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, I'd just ask you about the -- if you like, the -- the executive chain relating to these bodies. First of all, would you agree that Municipal Boards claimed and liked to exercise a fairly high degree of autonomy from the higher bodies within the party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have such authority; I believe that that was the case. But they were very independent when it came to local issues. At the same time, in accordance with the party's statute, they were obliged to implement the policies of the higher bodies; they were obliged to implement party policies. They had a certain degree of independence when it came to dealing with local issues, but, on the other hand, in accordance with the statue, they had to abide by the decisions of those above them, and higher level bodies also had to respect their programme and the statute. So the programme and the statute was binding on these higher level bodies, as well. In each and every party, a balance has to be struck between centralisation and decentralisation. You have to try and reconcile these two principles, in a certain sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Neskovic, you -- you had all this experience of visiting municipalities. Was the pattern also perhaps a perfectly natural one, that what you saw on paper, as to the -- the -- the way it was supposed to work, was very imperfectly reflected in what happened in practice? I'm talking about the chain of command, if you like, down from the Main Board to the Regional Board to the Municipal Board to the local committees. It -- it never -- never worked as neatly as it looked on paper, did it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'd have to examine individual cases and examine each individual municipality. It depended on the people in leadership positions in the municipalities; some had a tendency to act more independently. In the case of the Municipal Board in Banja Luka, that board did not really feel it had to respect party discipline. There were other such Municipal Boards. It all depended on the people in charge of those Municipal Boards; it depended on their political capacity. But the party structure prescribed in the statute was somewhat disturbed by the unlimited possibility that representatives of Municipal Boards had to go and see Mr. Karadzic, speak to him in person, and inform him of problems they had encountered. Karadzic might tacitly authorise them to act in a different way, and they would then do so. So the contact that Municipal Boards had with the president himself was the sort of contact that they were quite capable of establishing; it was possible for them to have such contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time we got to late 1991 and early 1992, Mr. Neskovic, such instructions or directions as went down to the municipal level, did they come from Dr. Karadzic, as the president, or from the Main Board, or from the Executive Board, or some mixture, or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very difficult and complex question that you have put to me, and I would need some time to answer it. It's an extremely important and extremely difficult question. If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that it's a good question to leave the witness to reflect upon, and I could return to it very first thing tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the clock and considering that it's always good to have time for reflection, I follow your suggestion. Before we'll adjourn, I'd first like to instruct the witness that he should not speak with anyone about the testimony you've given until now and that you'll give when you'll be back with us tomorrow. We'd like to have you back at 9.00 in the morning, same courtroom. And perhaps you'd first escort the witness out of the courtroom, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you give us an impression on how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I certainly wouldn't finish in the first session, Your Honour. I would -- I would hope and aim to finish -- it would probably be rather late in second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a look, then, how that fits into our -- I'll have to do the calculation. I've got no idea whether it fits in well or not. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not all that far off, I think, Your Honour, from a very rough calculation in my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But again, I hope Your Honours are not going to approach it with a too rigid calculating approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know my constant fight with my love for and the testing of arithmetics. Mr. Krajisnik, would you have, as far as you could imagine now, have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've told Mr. Stewart what questions should be put to this witness, and whatever he puts to the witness I won't have to. And I think that here we are talking about a certain number of important questions. We must get facts established through this witness. And he can be -- this witness can be of great assistance to the Trial Chamber. I'm really unable to tell you how long it will take because I always take the leftovers, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which is -- and it's very pertinent, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik and I don't have anywhere near as many differences as might be thought. However, line 15 and line 16 exactly encapsulates the fundamental problem because if that is not giving directions to counsel about how to conduct the case, then I simply don't know what is. I ask what is left of the notion that counsel conducts the case. It's instructions given by counsel as to precisely what questions to ask and it being implicit that if he doesn't ask it, they will be asked anyway. And there it is, Your Honour. It just jumps off the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I had in my mind at that very moment - and I do not know whether it's a translation issue or not - I know that it's a very sensitive issue, but I was about to ask Mr. Krajisnik whether he meant what questions he would wish you to put to the witness. It might have been that he thought of it in this way. And let's not make a drama out of this one line at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not making a drama. But I can interpret that question in the light of many, many hours of discussion with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, I know what is meant, anyway, despite -- leaving aside the fact that it is, in fact, very obvious what it means as a matter of wording. That's exactly what it means because if I don't ask the questions, it's clearly stated there they will be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm being told -- I'm simply being told what to do. I'm being -- as counsel with the conduct of the case, I'm just being directed what to do. Really, Your Honour, perhaps I might as well just go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have all time for reflection until tomorrow morning. Mr. Tieger, is there anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In light of the time estimates, I would ask the Court to consider the possibility of an additional session tomorrow or Thursday. I suppose Thursday might be the safest, in -- in the sense that we might make up time or that the additional time might not be needed, but I'm a bit concerned about that. And I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's important to consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Thank you for your suggestion. I couldn't say that the Chamber had not thought about it without this suggestion. We'll adjourn until --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, I firmly would resist any suggestion of an additional session tomorrow. Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm doing these witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Thursday -- I'm certainly open minded about Thursday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I can cut that short. Yes. Well, if it had been on the mind of the Chamber, then it would be Thursday that was on the mind of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that. Thank you. That solves that, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of July, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
